newsitem.title: CHINA: Gold rush in southern China -- Deng's legacy.
newsitem.headline: Gold rush in southern China -- Deng's legacy.

text.p: Deng Xiaoping ignited in southern China the biggest economic boom on earth.

For the first 30 years of Communist Party rule after 1949, the two basically agricultural provinces of Guangdong and Fujian were among China's poorest, left to languish while Beijing invested in the northeast and in the interior.
While emigrant natives of both provinces prospered in exile across Asia and the Americas, their mainland kin sunk in poverty in their ancestral villages.
Deng, who died on Wednesday, changed all that.

After he took over in 1978, Deng used Guangdong as a cradle for economic reform, granting tax privileges to attract investment from neighbouring Hong Kong and allowing it to retain most of the tax revenues it generated.
He later extended the same privileges to Fujian, opposite Taiwan, to attract investors from the breakaway island.
The results were dramatic.
Guangdong's Gross Domestic Product in 1994 was 417.5 billion yuan ($50.3 billion), ranking first among all cities and provinces in China and more than 10 times the pre-1978 figure.
In 1994, its foreign trade was $96.66 billion, accounting for 41 percent of China's total. It attracted $9.4 billion in actual foreign investment, 28 percent of the national total.
Guangdong has three of China's four Special Economic Zones -- brainchilds of Deng's reform process -- and one of its two stock markets.

In 1994, Fujian's GDP reached 145 billion yuan ($17.5 billion), six times the 1978 figure. Its foreign trade in 1994 was $12.86 billion, ranking fourth in the nation, with $4 billion in actual foreign investment.
This spectacular growth has been largely outside the state sector, in foreign-invested, private and collective firms, all banned in pre-1978 China.
Many of the new factories were export-oriented, moved by their owners from Hong Kong and Taiwan to make use of the much lower wages in mainland China.
"Deng's success was to tap the enormous economic potential of Hong Kong and later Taiwan, which were looking for cheaper places to manufacture their goods," a Chinese economist said.
"What he gave Guangdong and Fujian was not money but policies, in investment and tax, so that they would develop under their own steam, without money from Beijing."
Guangdong and Fujian would not enjoy their present prosperity without Deng, said Zhang Xianyang, a researcher with the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.
"It was he who saw that China had to use capital from abroad and that investors from Hong Kong were the best potential providers," he said.
"It was Deng who protected the two provinces in the 1980s from conservatives in the leadership who opposed the preferential policies given to them," he said.
In early 1992, after many in Beijing had criticised the special economic zones as the return of capitalism, Deng defied poor health to tour Guangdong.
His visit, known as the "southern tour", sparked rapid economic growth nationwide.

The political result of this astonishing growth was that Guangdong became increasingly self-reliant for capital, giving Beijing less power over it and allowing it to finance ambitious projects such as a subway and expressways.
It also produced unwelcome side-effects, such as prostitution, drugs, gambling and gangsters.
Commenting on the future for Guangdong and Fujian, Zhang said: "One generation can only achieve one thing. Our grandsons can work to achieve justice and fairness."
